outline: Infectious and immunologic, including microbiologic and host response to insult
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Babesia species are intraerythrocytic protozoan parasites. In the United States, B. microti is the most common human species and is typically transmitted by Ixodes scapularis in the Northeast and upper Midwest. Infection can cause hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia; advanced age, asplenia or hyposplenia, and impaired immune function increase the risk for severe disease. Blood-smear microscopy can demonstrate intraerythrocytic parasites, including delicate ring forms and occasional tetrads; morphology alone does not establish the Babesia species.
vignette: A 67-year-old man presents in July with 5 days of fever, chills, profound fatigue, and dark urine. He underwent splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision 20 years ago. He lives in coastal Massachusetts and spends weekends hiking but has not traveled outside the United States. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F). Examination shows mild scleral icterus without rash. Laboratory studies show anemia, thrombocytopenia, increased indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and decreased haptoglobin. A manual review of a Wright-Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear shows delicate ring-shaped organisms within erythrocytes; several infected erythrocytes contain multiple ring forms, and an occasional tetrad is seen.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Malaria can cause fever, hemolytic anemia, and intraerythrocytic parasites, so it is a clinically important mimic. However, CDC recommends suspecting malaria particularly after exposure in a malaria-endemic area. This patient has no such travel history, while the combination of New England tick exposure, asplenia, and Babesia-compatible erythrocytic ring/tetrad forms more strongly supports babesiosis.

Anaplasmosis is an Ixodes-associated febrile illness that commonly causes leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. On peripheral smear, the characteristic finding when visible is morulae in granulocytes rather than intraerythrocytic ring forms.

Ehrlichiosis can cause fever, headache, malaise, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferases after tick exposure. It does not produce the intraerythrocytic ring/tetrad pattern described in this vignette.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tickborne bacterial illness that commonly presents with fever and headache and often develops a rash; thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia can occur. It does not cause intraerythrocytic protozoan ring/tetrad forms.
key_expl: This patient most likely has babesiosis. He has a summer febrile illness in an endemic northeastern US setting, laboratory evidence of hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia, prior splenectomy, and intraerythrocytic parasites on peripheral smear. CDC identifies asplenia as a major risk factor for severe babesiosis and recommends manual peripheral-smear review in suspected acute infection. CDC laboratory criteria include direct identification of intraerythrocytic Babesia organisms on a stained blood smear; Babesia blood smears characteristically can show delicate ring forms, multiple infection of erythrocytes, and occasional tetrad forms.
objective: Recognize babesiosis in a patient with compatible tick exposure, hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, especially when asplenia is present and peripheral smear demonstrates intraerythrocytic Babesia forms.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical Overview of Babesiosis
sources.support: CDC describes hemolytic anemia and flu-like symptoms, identifies asplenia/hyposplenia and advanced age as risk factors for severe disease, notes thrombocytopenia in acute illness, and recommends manual peripheral-blood-smear review to detect Babesia parasites.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: How Babesiosis Spreads
sources.support: CDC states that B. microti spreads through Ixodes scapularis (blacklegged/deer tick) bites and that U.S. babesiosis occurs most commonly in the Northeast and Midwest, often during warmer months.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Babesiosis 2025 Case Definition
sources.locator: Clinical Criteria; Laboratory Criteria — Confirmatory Laboratory Evidence
sources.support: CDC lists anemia and thrombocytopenia among clinical criteria and identifies direct visualization of intraerythrocytic Babesia organisms on Giemsa/Wright/Wright-Giemsa-stained blood smear or Babesia DNA detection by nucleic-acid testing as confirmatory laboratory evidence.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Laboratory Diagnosis of Babesiosis — Babesia spp. Bench Aid

sources.locator: Basic guidelines; Babesia morphology — Rings; tetrad forms
sources.support: CDC describes delicate, pleomorphic Babesia ring forms, multiple infection of red blood cells, and occasional classic tetrad forms; CDC DPDx also cautions that Babesia species cannot be identified to species level by morphology alone.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Evaluation and Diagnosis of Malaria
sources.locator: What to know; Diagnosis; Thick and thin blood smears
sources.support: CDC recommends considering malaria in febrile patients with recent exposure in a malaria-endemic area and confirms that malaria is diagnosed with parasite testing including thick and thin blood smears.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Anaplasmosis
sources.locator: Blood-smear microscopy during the first week of illness
sources.support: CDC states that peripheral smear may reveal Anaplasma morulae in granulocytes, distinguishing the relevant smear finding from intraerythrocytic Babesia forms.
